planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for the richest purple color; this cultivar, selected in Belgium in the 1930s, is one of the most widely planted purple-leaved shade trees in North America.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the deep maroon-purple foliage holds its color through summer better than most purple-leaved maples and turns a muted bronze before dropping in fall. It tolerates urban conditions, compacted soil, and road salt better than most maples, which drove its enormous popularity as a street and lawn tree through the mid-to-late 20th century. Note that Norway maple seeds prolifically and is classified as invasive in parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States, so some regions restrict or discourage new plantings. Its dense, shallow-rooted canopy casts heavy shade, making it difficult to grow turf or other plants beneath it.

planting.note: Sow cleaned seed outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Amur maple tolerates extreme cold and poor soils better than almost any other ornamental maple.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun for the best fall color and densest form, though it tolerates part shade and a wide pH range. This small, multi-stemmed tree native to northeastern Asia is prized for its exceptional cold hardiness, fragrant spring flowers, and brilliant scarlet-red fall foliage that often outshines Japanese maples in colder climates where those are not reliably hardy. It is frequently used as a windbreak, hedge, or specimen tree on the northern Great Plains and in prairie regions. Like Norway maple, Amur maple can self-seed aggressively and is listed as invasive in several states, so check local guidance before planting.

planting.note: Collect and sow acorns in fall shortly after they drop, pressing about 1 inch deep into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; this red-oak-group species germinates the following spring without extended stratification.

directions: Plant in dry to average, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; Northern Pin Oak (sometimes called Hill's Oak) is closely related to the pin oak but is better adapted to dry, sandy, and rocky upland sites across the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region rather than the wet bottomlands pin oak prefers. Its deeply lobed, bristle-tipped leaves turn red to reddish-brown in fall, and its small, bitter acorns are an important food source for wildlife. It develops a strongly pyramidal to rounded crown with persistent lower branches and is valued for tolerating poor, droughty soils where many other oaks struggle.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns directly in fall in well-drained, dry, alkaline soil in full sun; downy oak is highly tolerant of drought and limestone soils once established and resents being transplanted after its taproot develops.

directions: Plant in dry, well-drained, often calcareous soil in full sun; downy oak takes its common name from the fine, soft pubescence covering its young shoots and the undersides of its lobed leaves, a trait that distinguishes it from the closely related sessile oak. Native across southern and central Europe, it is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant deciduous oaks, thriving on dry limestone hillsides and in Mediterranean garrigue landscapes where few other deciduous trees persist. It is a modest-sized, often gnarled and picturesque tree, slow-growing, and valued in dry-climate and xeric landscape plantings for its resilience rather than for ornamental flash.
